title: Scalar and vector quantities
prior_knowledge_summary: Every physical quantity is reported with a numerical magnitude and an appropriate unit.
Students can estimate physical quantities and use SI units and prefixes.
Students can distinguish precision, accuracy and resolution.
Students can convert between absolute, fractional and percentage uncertainty and combine simple uncertainties.
new_learning: A scalar quantity has magnitude only.
A vector quantity has magnitude and direction.
Both scalar and vector physical quantities have a magnitude and an appropriate unit.
Common quantities can be classified by asking whether a direction is required to specify them completely.
not_yet_taught: Applications belonging to later Physics topics.

learning_outcomes.text: understand the difference between scalar and vector quantities and give examples of scalar and vector quantities included in the syllabus

visual_planning.reason: Six figures make the missing-direction puzzle visible, contrast the two controlled definitions, classify familiar quantities by a decision test, expose two common misconceptions and finish with a complete-record checklist.
visual_planning.style: rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch

blocks.title: Two displays show 18 m s⁻¹, but do they say the same thing?
content: A bicycle computer shows speed = 18 m s⁻¹. A navigation display shows velocity = 18 m s⁻¹ east. The numerical magnitude and unit match, yet only one display tells us where the motion is directed.
Imagine the bicycle turns around while keeping the same reading of 18 m s⁻¹. Its speed is unchanged, but its velocity is different because the direction has changed.
This is why physics separates quantities that need only a magnitude from quantities that also need a direction.

figure.purpose: Create the need for the scalar-vector distinction by showing identical magnitudes with different completeness
figure.brief: Draw a rectangular white-paper teacher sketch with two simple display cards. The left card reads speed 18 m s^-1 beside a bicycle. The right card reads velocity 18 m s^-1 east beside an east-pointing arrow. Below, sketch the bicycle turned west while the speed display remains 18 m s^-1. Use blue for magnitude and orange for direction. Do not use the words scalar or vector.
figure.alt_text: A speed display gives only 18 metres per second while a velocity display also gives the direction east.

blocks.title: A scalar is complete without a direction
content: Definition to learn: a scalar quantity is a physical quantity that has magnitude only.
Magnitude means numerical size. The unit still matters, so a scalar report such as mass = 2.4 kg contains a number and a unit, but no direction is required.
Time, mass, temperature, energy, speed, distance, power and work are scalar quantities. Turning around does not create a north-facing mass or a west-facing temperature.
A second example is a stopwatch reading of 12.0 s. The duration is completely specified by its magnitude and unit. Adding a compass direction would not describe the duration more fully.

controlled_definition.accepted_definition: a physical quantity that has magnitude only

figure.purpose: Show that different scalar examples are complete with a magnitude and unit alone
figure.brief: Create a colourful hand-drawn comparison strip on white paper with four cards: 12.0 s, 2.4 kg, 290 K and 35 J. Under each, show a small tick beside magnitude plus unit. Leave a crossed-out empty compass box to show that direction is not required. Keep labels short and do not introduce equations.
figure.alt_text: Time, mass, temperature and energy cards are complete with a magnitude and unit and no direction.

blocks.title: A vector also needs a direction
content: Definition to learn: a vector quantity is a physical quantity that has magnitude and direction.
A report of displacement = 6.0 m is incomplete because many final positions are 6.0 m from the start. Displacement = 6.0 m north is complete because it supplies both magnitude and direction.
Velocity, displacement, acceleration, force, momentum and weight are vector quantities. For each one, reversing the direction changes the physical quantity even if its magnitude stays the same.
A second example is a 5.0 N force. The same magnitude can push a trolley left or right, producing physically different directed forces. A direction is therefore essential to the force report.

controlled_definition.accepted_definition: a physical quantity that has magnitude and direction

figure.purpose: Make direction visibly necessary for a complete vector description
figure.brief: Draw two small white-paper panels. In the first, place a start dot with several possible end dots all 6.0 m away and label 6.0 m incomplete. Then show one north-pointing arrow labelled 6.0 m north complete. In the second, show equal 5.0 N arrows pushing a trolley left and right. Use distinct colours for magnitude labels and arrow directions.
figure.alt_text: A magnitude alone leaves several possible displacement directions, while a magnitude plus direction specifies one vector.

blocks.title: Use one question to classify a quantity
content: Ask: is a magnitude and unit enough to specify this physical quantity completely? If yes, it is scalar. If a direction is also required, it is vector.
For power, a value such as 60 W is complete. Power tells us the rate of energy transfer and does not point north or south, so power is scalar.
For momentum, 4.0 kg m s⁻¹ is not complete. Momentum follows a direction of motion, so the report needs a direction and momentum is vector.

The same decision works in a mixed list. Energy, time and temperature are scalar. Acceleration, force and momentum are vector. Memorised examples help, but the direction test explains why each classification is correct.

figure.purpose: Give students a reusable classification route rather than an unstructured list to memorise
figure.brief: Create a hand-drawn decision tree on a rectangular white page. Start with physical quantity, then ask magnitude plus unit enough? Route yes to scalar examples power, energy and time. Route no, direction also needed, to vector examples momentum, force and acceleration. Use green and purple branches and small simple icons, with generous white space.
figure.alt_text: A decision tree classifies quantities by whether magnitude and unit alone are sufficient or direction is also required.

blocks.title: The story and the unit do not decide the category
content: It can feel natural to call every quantity in a moving-object story a vector. That fails because the story may contain scalar quantities such as time, mass, speed, distance, energy, power and work alongside vector quantities such as velocity, acceleration, force and momentum.
The unit alone is also not a reliable label. Speed and velocity both use m s⁻¹, but speed needs magnitude only while velocity needs magnitude and direction.
Use the physical meaning, not the surrounding story or the unit. Ask whether reversing direction while keeping the magnitude would change the quantity being described.

figure.purpose: Correct the belief that motion contexts or shared units automatically determine scalar or vector status
figure.brief: Draw a split teacher-sketch page. On the left, show a moving trolley surrounded by mixed labels time, speed, force and momentum, sorted into two small baskets labelled magnitude only and magnitude plus direction. On the right, show speed and velocity cards both carrying m s^-1, but only velocity has an arrow. Add one note: meaning decides.
figure.alt_text: A moving-object context contains both scalars and vectors, and speed and velocity share a unit despite belonging to different categories.

blocks.title: Check a field-data screen for completeness
content: A field-data screen lists temperature = 289 K, observation time = 60 s, wind velocity = 12 m s⁻¹ west and sensor displacement = 3.0 m.
Temperature and time are scalars, so their numerical magnitudes and units make those records complete. Wind velocity is a vector, and its west direction is present, so that record is also complete.
Displacement is a vector, but the record gives no direction. A complete report could be displacement = 3.0 m upward if that matches the actual movement. Some physically correct direction is required.
Notice the order of the check: identify the physical quantity, decide scalar or vector, then check magnitude, unit and, for a vector, direction. No vector addition is needed.

figure.purpose: Model a complete three-stage audit of scalar and vector records without introducing vector operations
figure.brief: Create a rectangular white-paper annotated checklist with four field-data cards for temperature, observation time, wind velocity and sensor displacement. Add columns magnitude, unit and direction if needed. Tick the complete fields and circle the missing direction for displacement. End with a small corrected card reading 3.0 m upward. Use hand-drawn blue, orange and green marks.
figure.alt_text: A checklist shows that the displacement record lacks a direction while the scalar records and westward velocity record are complete.

blocks.title: Magnitude belongs to both; direction separates them
content: Both scalar and vector physical quantities have a magnitude and an appropriate unit. Direction is the extra property required by a vector.
For a scalar, magnitude plus unit is complete. For a vector, report magnitude plus unit plus direction.
Classify by physical meaning: would changing only the direction change the quantity? If yes, it is vector. If no direction is part of the quantity, it is scalar.
In this lesson we identify and report scalar and vector quantities. The next lesson will teach how coplanar vectors are added and subtracted, so no vector combination method is assumed yet.
